ANNUAL CONVENTION HELD AT
ANN ARBOR
By R. Timothy Leedy, Phi '57
"O
NE of the most successful Conven
tions in the history of the Frater
nity," was the general verdict of those who
attended the Convention held with the Phi
Chapter on
September 6 and 7. The at
tendance was excellent, no
Chapter being
unrepresented, and approximately 190
Brethren were
present at various times
throughout the Convention.
The smoothness and efiBciency which
characterized the business sessions and
social events were the result of careful,
long-term planning and preparation on the
part of the Executive Council on the one
hand and the Phi Chapter and the Phi
Corporation on the other.
BUSINESS MEETINGS
The business meetings of the Conven
tion, although not the most "popular" of
the many activities, were
highly successful.
Attendance by the delegates was excellent
and many non-delegates were present for
the proceedings. The four sessions of the
business meetings were held in the spa
cious Strauss House Assembly Room in the
same
building that housed the delegates.
The facihties proved to be exceptionally
good since there was a
great deal of room
and other advantages, such as sound
equipment.
The first meeting was held on Thurs
day morning and most of the time was oc
cupied with setting up the program for
the next three sessions. Donald A. Fink
beiner, Phi '17, President of the Phi Corpo
ration, called the meeting to order and
extended the greetings of the Phi Chapter
to the Convention. The meeting was then
turned over to Benjamin T. Burton, Chi
'21, President of the Executive Council.
Brother Burton proceeded to organize the
committees in which the business of the
Convention would be discussed. It was
Michael A. Lynch, Phi '56 and
Henry E. Bodman, Phi '96
generally felt that the committee system
used was most efficient, since much un
necessary discussion on the floor of the Con
vention was eliminated in this manner
and more work accomphshed.
At the afternoon session several reports
were submitted by committees and mem
bers of the Executive Council. The invita
tion extended by the Psi Chapter to enter
tain the 1957 Convention was of special
interest to aU members of the Fraternity.
The invitation was
accepted by the Con
vention. The Upsilon Chapter extended
a similar invitation to the 1958 Conven
tion.
On Friday morning the meeting began
with reports on
scholarship by various
Chapters. Those Chapters whose records
were
superior reported to the Convention

the systems they used to achieve their suc
cess and those Chapters whose records
were
poor reported their present condi
tion and what steps were
being taken to
remedy their standing. The Upsilon Chap
ter received the award for the highest
scholastic standing. The Epsilon Nu Chap
ter was
given the award for the Chapter
showing the greatest scholastic improve
ment and the Theta Theta Chapter also
received congratulations for its scholastic
improvement. Following the scholarship
report and awards resolutions, in the inter
est of scholarship for all Psi Upsilon Chap
ters, the two following resolutions were
passed:
RESOLVED: That, since academic stand
ards, times and methods of rushing and pledg
ing differ at each college and university, many
of the problems in connection therewith are
of such a nature as. to require local and indi
vidual attention and solution; and
RESOLVED: That, nevertheless, certain
guidance along the following lines should be
recommended to all of the Chapters, and,
following these guidances, which are herewith
submitted is strongly recommended:
A. Due and thorough inquiry should be
made relative to the previous academic
records of prospective pledges, and the
results of such inquiry made available
to all prospective pledges, and the re
sults of such inquiry made available to
all members before such members are
required to vote on
prospective pledges;
B. The utmost care should be used to avoid
pledging men whose previous records
cast doubt upon their ability to do satis
factory academic workj
C. Individual Chapters should estabhsh
minimum academic requirements for
pledging and initiation, since the trouble
with the academic standing of some of
our Chapters lies in the selection of
new members;
D. Each Chapter should institute a
study
plan for pledges.
On Friday afternoon the resolution was
adopted to establish a committee under
the Executive Council to act as a
clearing
house for further expansion of the Fra
ternity which will report any progress
made in the area to each Chapter at least
once every six months. At the conclusion
of the meeting the Committee on Ritual
and Tradition conducted a formal Chapter
meeting in accordance with the ritual of
the Fraternity. This meeting was con
ducted to illustrate to the delegates the
dignified ritual which each Chapter should
follow.
In retrospect, it seems that the business
meetings of the past Convention were
extremely successful. They were charac
terized by cooperation on the part of all
the delegates and the work at hand was
undertaken in a
highly efficient manner.
All active members of the Fraternity owe
much thanks to our loyal alumni for their
hard work, close cooperation, and wonder
ful enthusiasm in handfing the many de
tails which are involved in operating a
fraternity on a national basis.
THURSDAY NOON LUNCHEON
After the first business meeting which
had got the official business of the Conven
tion off to a
hasty but eflScient beginning,
the Brothers found just enough time for a
leisurely walk through the impressive law
quadrangle before their arrival at the
Michigan Union where luncheon was to
be served. Upon being seated in the com
fortable Anderson Room of the Union,
the delegates and guests were served with
generous portions of cold ham, turkey and
potato salad by several typically pretty
Michigan coeds. Brother Donald A. Fink
beiner, Phi '17, proved himself a
genial
toastmaster as he introduced to the dele
gates Mr. Walter Rea, Dean of Men, Mr.
Wilham Cross, Assistant to the Dean of
Men, and a
very good friend to the Inter-

fraternity Council, and Dr. Harlan Hatcher,
President of the University of Michi
gan. Dr. Hatcher spoke of his fond asso
ciation with our
Fraternity and had some
very laudable and interesting things to say
concerning the fraternity system in gen
eral. (A more detailed summary of his
comments follows.) Dr. Hatcher not only
made a fine impression on those in the
room who heard his comments, but those
who lingered after the luncheon was over
just long enough to meet and talk to him,
if for only a short time, carried away with
them the memory of a man of great depth
and personal warmth who is exemplary of
the Michigan tradition.
PRESIDENT HARLAN
HATCHER'S SPEECH
Highhght of Thursday's luncheon in the
newly opened wing of the Michigan
Union was the address given by Dr. Har
lan Hatcher, President of the University
of Michigan.
Dr. Hatcher opened his remarks with
warm reminiscences of his long friendship
with Brother Earl Babst, Iota-Phi '93,
whom he has known for many years. Con
tinuing his address to the Brothers assem
bled for lunch. President Hatcher singled
out several aspects of modern college life
with which fraternities ought to be par
ticularly acquainted.

quarter of
today's college students are marriedpointing up the higher average agfe of

ence on the Michigan Interfraternity

the achievements of fraternity men in re
cent
years-achievements which he feels

ing criticisms of fraternity living.

THURSDAY EVENING DINNER
"Done with the joys of duty," at least
for that day, the Brothers now looked for
ward to "the joys of the night" as busses
carried them to the spacious surroundings
of the Washtenaw Country Club. Dinner
was
preceded by an excellent social hour,
and was chmaxed by a fine meal of roast
beef.
As dinner drew to a close. Brother John
Calvin, Phi '56, called the assembly to
order and proceeded to distinguish him
self as
anything but a
story-telling toastmaster.
Full justice was
given to
John's abihty
later as he introduced once
again Brother
LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, who introduced
to Brother Calvin the art of story-telling.
Brother Charles Seaver, Psi '21, was also
called upon to say a few words. Brother
Calvin then introduced Brother Tim Leedy,
Phi '57, President of the Michigan Inter
fraternity Council. Tim's comments were
very pointed, and concerned the role the
fraternities are
playing and will play in a
society of the future. Brother Leedy's mes
sage has been summarized below. From
that point on the evening developed into
a social hour, with many Brothers seeing
familiar faces and renewing old friendships
while other Brothers were
making those
acquaintances that would someday be
old.
R. TIMOTHY LEEDY'S SPEECH
Brother Leedy's topic was a
timely
one, Complacency and the changing scene
on
campus:
"For nearly a century and a
quarter the
traditions that are Psi U have richly added
meaning to the hves of its brotherhood. Over
most of these years the college scene has
changed gradually, but the Depression and
the Second World War accelerated the pace
of this alteration tremendously. The bulk of
college freshmen are no longer youngsters
from families with a tradition of college
education extending back for generations. A
growing percentage of incoming college stu
dents do not have the background of a specific
and longstanding fraternity affiliation�a mark
which was characteristic of many prospective
fraternity men in days gone by.
"A knowledge of specific fratemities is no
longer expected to have been instilled in the
incoming freshman before leaving home. He
is given a rush period of anywhere from a
week to a semester to evaluate fraternities
for himself. Nevertheless, an
increasing in
fluence on his rushing decisions is the fre
quency with which he had heard of this or
that fraternity prior to his arrival at school.
"Unhke many younger organizations, Psi U
refuses to attain prominence through helterskelter chapter growth. But Psi U's can no
longer afford to depend on the strength of
family ties to assure in itself the calibre and
numbers of their chapters. An increasing
number of young men of Psi U calibre are
being drawn into our bonds almost solely on
the observable merits of our individual chap
ters.
"This situation means that more than ever
before Psi U is being measured against Houses
which 25 and 50 years ago were not even
considered poor competition by many of our
Chapters. It means that many fratemities
larger nationally than Psi U undoubtedly have
counteracted the traditional quality of Psi U
in the minds of many incoming freshmen with
their sheer size and number of chapters.
"It means that as never before Psi U's
cannot afford to be lethargic. It means if the
greatness of our Brotherhood is to endure it
will do so in the sweat that comes from
staging a successful rush, in the thoroughness
of a
pledge training that truly integrates the
prospective Brother into the fraternity and
campus hfe, in the vitahty which character
izes a smooth mnning chapter organization,
and in the elan which promotes those mean
ingful and rewarding ties between active and
alumni brothers. It is on this battle plain

that our traditions will survive or
perish. And
here, on this field, there is no room for
complacency."
FRIDAY NOON PROGRAM
With the usual fun and joking that pre
vailed throughout the entire three days,
the Convention picture was taken after
which an informal buffet type luncheon
was held at the Chapter House. The buffet,
consisting of cold cuts and potato salad,
was not only tasty and filling, but also
represented the artistry with which the
Phi's cook, Jesse Tuggle, goes about his
work. Following the buffet, the delegates
filed off to the final business meeting.
FRIDAY EVENING BANQUET
The entire Convention attendance,
plus many other notable alumni were
present at this final gathering at the Bar
ton Hills Country Club. This being the
last time when the undergraduate dele
gates could be together at this Conven
tion, they in particular took advantage of
the opportunity for improving acquaint
ances and friendships formed during the
past two days.
Following the excellent dinner of either
swordfish steak or fried chicken, Michael
Lynch, Phi '56, commenced his duties as
Master of Ceremonies. Mike introduced
the notable Brothers at the dinner table,
among them LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01,
Past President of the Executive Council,
Benjamin T. Burton, Chi '21, its present
President, and Henry E. Bodman, Phi '96,
President of the Phi at the time of the
63rd National Convention, held with the
Phi in 1896.
Following Brother Bodman's remarks,
Brother D. Bowen King, Theta Theta '57,
presented the aforementioned scholarship
awards to the Upsilon and Epsilon Nu
Chapters. Next introduced was William

plause.
After the ovation, goodnights were said,
and some of the Brothers gathered in
various bedrooms for further conversation,
while others sought their beds and much
needed rest.
SUMMARY
The business of the Fraternity was dis
patched with great efficiency, and the
social events were completely successful.
More important than the recorded ac
complishments of a Convention are the
new friendships made, and a tone, an in
describable something that is generated
within the individual, that he may take
into his heart as his and also convey to
others, the Brotherhood of Psi Upsilon.

Life with Salt on the Side:
Confessions of a Brooklynite
"TN what part of Brooklyn were you
X born?" That is a question I am fre
quently asked. I was not born in the
beautiful borough acrbss the bridge. I
was born in Manhattan. So was my
mother. And so was her mother. How
ever, I was brought up in Brooklyn.
Every time I say I was brought up in
Brooklyn, a Bostonian sends me a tele
gram that I should say I was "reared"
in Brooklyn. In Brooklyn you are
"brought up." In Boston you are
"reared." Anyway, we moved across the
bridge when I was seven. I am a gradu
ate of P.S. No. Two and Commercial
H.S. (later Alexander Hamilton High)
of Brooklyn.
On the Bay
We lived in South Brooklyn on the
outskirts of Bay Ridge. From our socalled "bay window" we could see the
Statue of Liberty. We had binoculars and
a telescope we used to get close-up
views of the many ocean liners sailing
d^wn the bay. It was a wonderful neigh
borhood. Great place for kids. A very
friendly place in those days.
My mother never cared much for
Birooklyn. She made the best of residing
in Bay Ridge because she thought it
was a good place for children. She was
interested iti sports but never became a
supporter of the Dodgers. She was a
Giant fan right up to the end.
Kindly subscribers comphment me
on having a wide variety of interests.
That is the result of early environment.
Within a radius of five miles of our
New York Journal-

baseball park, three major class race
tracks. Coney Island, big time vaude
ville at the Orpheum and several thea
tres on the so-called "subway circuit"
presenting legitimate plays. Also three
theatres presenting burlesque, one of
which was the celebrated show shop
known as "Watson's Cosy Corner." Less
than a half mile away was Ambrose
Park where the major circuses and Wild

Sports Centre
Bay Ridge was a great sports, cen
tre. There were a number of boxing
clubs in the vicinity. At Coney Island,
world's heavyweight boxing bouts were
held. At the Crescent A. C, featuring
amateur sports, were played golf, la
crosse, tennis, baseball and football. The
club also had an eight-oared crew. At the
Prospect Park Parade Grounds polo was
regularly played.
When about 17, I started going to
school and college in New England and
never lived regularly in Brooklyn after
that. I spent eight years in New England.
My baseball position was first base.
I graduated from Wesleyan University,

nationally syndicated columnist for 17
years. My father was born in London,
England, but came to this country at

PSI U'S AND THE FORWARD PASS!
WHO THREW FIRST SPIRAL PASS?
By Lawbence Robinson, Delta Tau Delta Fraternity '24
[EDITOR'S NOTE: A Delta Tau Delt brings to
light the fact that three Psi U's had a part in
starting the Forward Pass! Amos Alonzo Stagg,
Beta '88, Lucius Horatio Bigelow, Jr., Beta '08 and
John Reed Kilpatrick, Beta 'II. Lawrence Robin
son, Delta Tau Delta '24, at Syracuse University
is the football authority of the New York WorldTelegram and Sun. He is Vice Chairman of the
Football Coach of the Vear Committee.]
AS
AMERICAN college football ob-
, serves the 50th year of the legalized
forward pass this fall, the question arises
not so much about who threw the first
historic pass but who discovered the art
of throwing it spirally for distance, thus
aiming it instead of putting it up for
grabs.
Into this controversy, there enter at
least two names, perhaps three.
On the records, the mightiest pass of
that 1906 season flew from Bradbury Rob
inson, St. Louis U. halfback, to end John
